title: Student-Led Movement Topples Serbia's Longtime Leader
summary:
Brazil was not the only country with dramatic election news this weekend. In Serbia, a small country in southeastern Europe with under seven million people, longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic lost a historic election on Sunday that brought down his government.

What makes this result extraordinary, experts say, is how it happened. The movement that defeated Vucic was led by students. It had no single leader. It was decentralized — spread out rather than run from the top — and digitally savvy, using online tools to organize. And it brought down a leader who held tight control over Serbia's economic and political power.

The protesters' main focus was corruption in government, an issue that is becoming a global concern. Vucic had once served in the cabinet of Slobodan Milosevic, a former Serbian leader. The student movement's win follows a recent election in Hungary that brought in a new leader who also fought corruption, and it is seen as a setback for Russia and China, two countries that strongly influenced Serbia.

This was not a race between Vucic and one rival candidate. It was a parliamentary election, meaning voters chose parties, not a single president. When polls showed his party losing badly, Vucic conceded peacefully — a move that surprised observers, who often expect powerful leaders to cling to power. There was an hour when Serbia's electoral commission did not release results, but officials then acknowledged the scale of the loss.

The big question now is what comes next. If the student-led movement, which has no single leader, cannot form a government, Vucic's side still holds many levers of power and could fight another day. For now, though, the win belongs to the people of Serbia — and to a young movement that connected the dots with youth protests across Europe.
why_it_matters: It shows that a student-led movement can bring down a powerful leader. It also matters because corruption in government is becoming a global concern.
